sections.heading: Asking the Spirit to show me the truth about my sin
sections.text: Holy Spirit, giver of grace and comfort, come and do what I cannot do for myself. Bring real repentance into my heart. Let me see my sin as it really is—not excused, not dressed up, not made small, but ugly and hateful because it is against God. Break through my numbness. Let the greatness of God and the mercy of God soften me, humble me, and draw me back to him.
theological_themes: The Holy Spirit convicts the heart and brings repentance.
Sin must be seen truthfully before it can be hated and forsaken.
God’s majesty and mercy together melt a hard heart.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus teaches that the Spirit exposes the world’s guilt concerning sin, righteousness, and judgment. This grounds the prayer’s request that the Spirit would reveal sin honestly rather than leaving the heart self-deceived.
Paul says God’s kindness is meant to lead people to repentance. The prayer asks not only for fear of sin, but for God’s mercy to soften the heart and draw it back to him.

sections.heading: Seeing my need and God’s readiness to save
sections.text: Show me the wreckage in me, but do not leave me staring at myself. Show me the help that is in God. Teach me to look at my Creator as the one who is able to save, willing to receive, and full of compassion toward me in Christ. Help me trust both his power and his love, and give myself to him without holding anything back.
theological_themes: Human ruin is answered by God’s saving power and mercy.
Faith rests in God’s ability and willingness to save.
True surrender gives the whole self to God.

scripture_references.connection: God calls people to look to him for salvation because he alone is God. This supports the movement from self-despair to confidence in God’s saving sufficiency.
Christ is able to save completely those who draw near to God through him. The prayer’s confidence in God’s power to save is anchored in Christ’s ongoing priestly work.
The father’s welcome of the returning son gives a biblical picture of God’s mercy toward the repentant. It illuminates the prayer’s image of God’s open-hearted readiness to receive.

sections.heading: Becoming a living display of grace
sections.text: Let my life bear your image more and more. Teach me to love your commands, to serve you gladly, and to belong to you in every part of my life. Make me, now and forever, a visible sign of what your grace can do—a life rescued by your victory, not by my strength.
theological_themes: Grace not only pardons but reshapes the believer’s life.
The redeemed life displays God’s victory over sin.
Obedience and service flow from saving grace.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes believers being transformed into the Lord’s image by the Spirit. This directly supports the prayer’s request to bear God’s image increasingly.
Salvation is by grace through faith, and believers are created in Christ for good works. The passage holds together grace, rescue, and a life of obedient service.

sections.heading: Being saved in Christ’s way, not mine
sections.text: Make me willing to be saved on your terms, not mine. Teach me to stop searching for something in myself that could make me acceptable to you. Let me find everything I need in Jesus. Help me not only to receive him at the beginning, but to keep walking with him—depending on him, staying close to him, becoming like him, and following him. I know my obedience is still imperfect, but keep me moving forward. Keep me from resenting the work, and teach me to value the rest you promise. Keep me from grumbling in hardship, and make me grateful for the grace that already holds me.
theological_themes: Christ is the believer’s whole sufficiency.
The Christian life continues by dependence on Christ, not self-reliance.
Growth in holiness is imperfect but persevering.
Trials are to be endured with trust rather than resentment.

scripture_references.connection: Paul urges believers who received Christ to continue walking in him, rooted and built up in him. This directly supports the prayer’s movement from receiving Christ to ongoing dependence and communion with him.
Paul admits he has not yet arrived, yet presses on toward Christ. This matches the prayer’s honest confession of imperfect obedience while still moving forward.
James teaches that trials can produce steadfastness and maturity. This supports the prayer’s request not to murmur under trials but to meet them with faith and gratitude.

sections.heading: Living by the faith that receives everything from Christ
sections.text: Give me the faith through which you save me, and let that same faith shape the whole of my life. Let me be saved by grace through faith, live each day by faith, know the joy that comes from trusting you, and do the work that faith produces. Since I have nothing in myself to boast in, let me find in Christ my wisdom, my righteousness, my holiness, and my redemption.
theological_themes: Faith is the means by which grace is received.
The believer continues to live, rejoice, and work by faith.
Christ supplies everything needed for salvation and godliness.

scripture_references.connection: This passage teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not human boasting, and that good works follow as God’s workmanship. It supports both receiving salvation by faith and living out the works faith produces.
Paul describes the Christian life as life lived by faith in the Son of God. This grounds the prayer’s desire not merely to begin by faith, but to live by faith daily.

Paul says Christ has become wisdom, righteousness, sanctification, and redemption for believers, leaving no room for boasting in ourselves. This directly supports the prayer’s final confession that everything needed is found in Christ.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original strongly emphasizes human inability and the Spirit’s initiative in repentance and faith, which reflects a Reformed/Puritan soteriological framework and may be doctrinally contested in some Christian traditions.
The image of being a “monument” and “trophy” of grace and victory could sound impersonal or triumphalistic today; it was retained in meaning as a life that visibly displays God’s grace and rescue.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Represent sin to me in its odious colours” was rendered as seeing sin without excuses or minimization, because the original asks for moral and spiritual clarity rather than merely emotional shame.
“His arms outstretched” and “his heart big for me” were interpreted as God’s merciful readiness to receive repentant sinners in Christ, not as a claim that God saves apart from repentance and faith.
“Saved in his way” was rendered as being saved on God’s terms rather than my own, preserving the original contrast between self-reliance and receiving everything in Jesus.
“Not complaining of labour, but valuing rest” was interpreted as persevering in the difficult obedience of discipleship while treasuring the rest God gives and promises.
